subject: science
passage: Bakers describe a dough's hydration as the weight of its water compared with the weight of its flour, so a dough with 75% hydration contains 75 grams of water for every 100 grams of flour. Wetter doughs often rise higher in the oven, but only up to a point, beyond which they spread instead. Baker and food scientist Henrik Dahl argues that this point depends on the flour: bread flour, which contains more of the proteins that form gluten, can hold more water before it stops rising than all-purpose flour can.

data.title: Height of Sourdough Loaves at Different Dough Hydrations

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Dahl's argument?

choices.A: At every hydration level tested, the bread-flour loaves were taller than the all-purpose loaves.
choices.B: At 85% hydration, loaves made with either kind of flour were shorter than at 80% hydration.
choices.C: Bread-flour loaves were tallest at 80% hydration, while all-purpose loaves were tallest at 75%.
choices.D: All-purpose loaves reached their greatest height at a higher hydration than bread-flour loaves did.

explanation.why: Dahl claims that the hydration at which loaves stop rising higher is greater for bread flour than for all-purpose flour. The choice must compare where each flour's loaves reach their peak height. Bread-flour loaves peak at 80% (10.1 centimeters), while all-purpose loaves peak at 75% (8.9 centimeters).
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it shows only that bread flour makes taller loaves, not that it reaches its peak at a higher hydration.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes only the drop after 80% and does not show that the two flours peak at different hydrations.
explanation.C: Correct. Bread flour kept rising up to 80% hydration, while all-purpose flour peaked at 75%, so bread flour can hold more water before it stops rising.
explanation.D: Incorrect. All-purpose loaves peaked at 75% and bread-flour loaves at 80%, so this reverses the data.
